sections.title: Lesson 7.1: Investment Risks (Systematic vs. Nonsystematic)
sections.overview: Investment risk is divided into systematic (nondiversifiable, market-wide) and nonsystematic (diversifiable, issuer/industry-specific) categories. Systematic risk cannot be eliminated through diversification — only hedged via derivatives or counter-moving assets. Nonsystematic risk is reduced by holding a diversified portfolio across issuers, industries, and asset classes.
key_concepts: SYSTEMATIC RISK — built into the market; cannot be diversified away.
Market Risk: when the overall market declines, diversified equity portfolios decline with it (measured by beta vs. S&P 500).
Interest Rate Risk: bond prices move inversely to interest rates; longer-duration bonds are more sensitive. Sometimes called 'market risk for bonds.'
Reinvestment Risk: when rates fall, proceeds from coupons, calls, or maturities must be reinvested at lower yields.
Inflation/Purchasing Power Risk: fixed income loses real value as prices rise; affects all fixed-income payments (bonds, fixed annuities, CDs).
Currency Risk: foreign-denominated investments lose value if the foreign currency weakens vs. the USD; quoted at spot rate.
Call Risk: callable bonds may be redeemed early when rates fall; leads to reinvestment risk. Treasuries are not callable; corporates/munis usually offer call protection.
Political/Sovereign Risk: instability of a country's government or its ability to service sovereign debt (especially emerging markets).
NONSYSTEMATIC RISK — unique to an issuer/industry; mitigated by diversification.
Default/Credit/Financial Risk: issuer fails to pay interest or principal; most relevant to debt securities.
Capital Risk: investor may not recover original principal (minimal for T-bills; high for options/DPPs).
Business Risk: poor management or operating decisions reduce earnings or cause company failure.
Prepayment Risk: borrowers (e.g., mortgage holders backing GNMAs) prepay principal when rates fall, forcing reinvestment at lower rates.
Liquidity/Marketability Risk: inability to sell quickly at a fair price (real estate, collectibles, thinly traded bonds).
Regulatory Risk: change in agency rules (FDA, EPA) hurts a company/industry.
Legislative Risk: a change in the LAW (e.g., tax code, luxury tax) impacts an investment. Distinguish from regulatory (agency rules).
Beta measures volatility vs. the market (S&P 500 = 1.00). Beta > 1.00 = more volatile; < 1.00 = less volatile. Beta is a measure of nonsystematic/relative risk.
rules: FINRA recognizes both systematic and nonsystematic risk categories in suitability analysis (Reg BI Care Obligation requires understanding of risks/rewards/costs).
formulas: Risk-Reward Axiom: Higher risk = higher potential reward AND higher potential loss; lower risk = lower potential reward.
Beta of the market (S&P 500) = 1.00; Security Beta > 1.00 = more volatile than market; < 1.00 = less volatile.
mnemonics: Systematic risks = 'PRIME-C': Purchasing power, Reinvestment, Interest rate, Market, Exchange (currency), Call.
Nonsystematic risks = 'BLRCP': Business, Liquidity, Regulatory/legislative, Credit (default), Prepayment.
'Cannot Diversify the System' — systematic risk is nondiversifiable.

sections.title: Lesson 7.2: Recommendations, Suitability, Regulation BI, and Market Benchmarks
sections.overview: A recommendation is any communication that reasonably could be viewed as a 'call to action' to buy, sell, or hold a security. Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), effective 6/30/2020, requires broker-dealers and associated persons to act in the retail customer's best interest when making a recommendation, satisfying four component obligations: Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance. Suitability depends on aligning the customer's financial and nonfinancial profile with appropriate investment products, and performance is judged against an appropriate benchmark index.
key_concepts: RECOMMENDATION DEFINITION: a communication that 'reasonably could be viewed as a call to action' influencing a purchase, sale, or hold of a specific security or strategy — includes explicit hold recommendations and account-type recommendations (e.g., open IRA, rollover).

CUSTOMER PROFILE — must collect: age, marital status, dependents, employment, income, net worth, liquid net worth, tax status, investment experience, investment objectives, time horizon, liquidity needs, and risk tolerance.
Financial Circumstances (quantifiable in dollars): income, home value, liquid net worth, debt payments, total debt.
Nonfinancial Circumstances: age, marital status, dependents, employment status, family employment.
INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES → SUITABLE PRODUCTS:
• Preservation of Capital/Safety → CDs, money market funds, fixed annuities, Treasuries, agencies, investment-grade corporates.
• Growth (Moderate) → common stock, blue-chip, defensive stocks, stock mutual funds.
• Aggressive Growth → tech stocks, sector funds, emerging markets.
• Income → bonds (NOT zero coupons), REITs, CMOs, preferred/utility stocks.
• Tax-Free Income → municipal bonds/funds, Roth IRA.
• High-Yield Income → below-investment-grade ('junk') bond funds.
• Liquidity → exchange-listed stocks, Nasdaq stocks, mutual funds, publicly traded REITs.
• Diversification → mutual funds, asset allocation/balanced funds.
• Speculation → options, DPPs, high-yield bonds, sector funds, commodities, futures, precious metals.

REGULATION BEST INTEREST (Reg BI) — effective 6/30/2020; under '34 Act; applies to broker-dealers and associated persons making recommendations to RETAIL customers (excludes institutional accounts: banks, S&Ls, insurance companies, registered investment companies).
Reg BI prohibits placing firm or associated person interest ahead of the retail customer's interest.
FOUR REG BI OBLIGATIONS:

1. DISCLOSURE OBLIGATION — full and fair written disclosure before/at time of recommendation: scope/terms of relationship, fees and costs, type/scope of services, material limitations on products recommended, and all material conflicts of interest.

2. CARE OBLIGATION — exercise reasonable diligence, care, skill; understand risks/rewards/costs; reasonable basis recommendation could be in some retail customer's best interest; customer-specific basis; series of recommendations not excessive.

3. CONFLICT OF INTEREST OBLIGATION (firm-level) — written policies to identify, mitigate, or eliminate conflicts; eliminate sales contests/quotas/bonuses tied to specific securities or specific types of securities within a limited period.
4. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION (firm-level) — written policies and procedures designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI as a whole.
USE OF 'ADVISER/ADVISOR' TITLE — presumptive Reg BI violation for a BD or AP not also registered as an IA/IA representative (requires Series 65 or 66).

FORM CRS (Customer Relationship Summary) — delivered to retail investors at the earlier of: entering into an IA contract OR opening a brokerage account. 2 pages for BD or IA; up to 4 pages for dual-registrants.
MAJOR MARKET BENCHMARKS:
• DJIA — 30 large-cap U.S. industrial stocks; price-weighted; most widely cited in popular press.
• S&P 500 — ~500 large U.S. companies; market-cap weighted; standard benchmark for overall U.S. market performance and large-cap portfolios.
• Russell 2000 — ~2,000 small-cap U.S. stocks; benchmark for small-company performance.
• Wilshire 5000 — broadest measure of U.S. equity market (~3,500 actual components).
• Nasdaq Composite — all Nasdaq-listed stocks; tech-heavy.
• Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Aggregate Bond Index ('the Agg') — composite benchmark for U.S. bond market.
• MSCI EAFE Index — developed-market equities outside U.S./Canada (Europe, Australasia, Far East); standard international equity benchmark.
rules: SEC Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) — Securities Exchange Act of 1934; effective June 30, 2020; retail customers only.
Form CRS — required relationship summary delivered to retail investors at/before account opening or advisory contract.

FINRA noncash compensation rules amended to comply with Reg BI: contests may continue, but incentives based on product type (e.g., mutual funds) must apply to ALL products of that type sold by the firm — not a single sponsor.
Reg BI excludes recommendations to institutional accounts (banks, S&Ls, insurance companies, registered investment companies).
mnemonics: Reg BI Four Obligations = 'DC³' or 'DCCC': Disclosure, Care, Conflict of interest, Compliance.
Recommendation test = 'Call to Action' — would it influence a customer to trade or hold a specific security?
Income objective avoids ZEROS — zero-coupon bonds pay NO current income.
Benchmark match: Large-cap → S&P 500; Small-cap → Russell 2000; Broad U.S. → Wilshire 5000; Bonds → Bloomberg Barclays Agg; International → MSCI EAFE; 30 blue chips → DJIA.
